span.label: A TERMINOLOGY, AND THE PROCEDURE FOR AGREEING ONE - ten sequential steps, 1,094 members invited, 87 responding, and a 75% bar set before the vote, to settle what `sedentary behavior`, `stationary behavior`, `sitting`, `reclining`, `lying`, `standing` and `screen time` each mean
span.quote: A series of sequential processes were employed in an effort to derive consensus definitions for key terms in sedentary behavior research (Fig. 1 ). These processes included i) a literature search, ii) establishment of a Steering Committee of SBRN members, iii) invitation to all SBRN members to participate in the consensus project, iv) selecting a list of key terms, v) developing a conceptual model, vi) drafting definitions for key terms, vii) collecting input and feedback on the conceptual model and draft definitions from participating SBRN members, viii) compiling input and finalizing (reaching consensus on) the conceptual model and definitions, ix) preparing the manuscript with sign-off by all participants, x) and finally disseminating project results through publication and presentation.

span.label: what the field's key terms should mean, when its own literature defines the central one at MET ceilings from 1.5 to 2.0 and three papers give no number at all
span.quote: As this field of research has grown, so too has confusion over the definition of sedentary behavior (see Table 1 for a sample of definitions) and other related terms (e.g., screen time, sedentary behavior patterns, bouts, breaks) [ 4 , 7 , 17 – 22 ]. For example, Altenburg and Chinapaw [ 17 ] recently recommended that to advance the field of sedentary behavior epidemiology, standardized procedures for accelerometer data collection and data reduction should be defined; standardized operational definitions of sedentary bouts and breaks are needed; sedentary bouts should be operationally defined as a minimum period of uninterrupted sedentary time; total time accumulated in sedentary bouts per day (or per week) should be calculated rather than using average bout duration; and the best mathematical adjustment that converts accelerometer data into sedentary patterns should be further explored.

span.label: consensus definitions for ten terms plus the usage of `bouts`, `breaks` and `interruptions`, with caveats and examples written for all age groups and functional abilities, and a conceptual model positioning the terms
span.quote: The survey asked participants to assess the clarity of, and agreement with, the conceptual model and proposed definitions (using a five point scale from strongly agree to strongly disagree), while also providing an opportunity for general comments. Consensus was determined a priori to have been achieved if ≥75% of respondents strongly agreed or somewhat agreed with a particular question (see Additional file 1 : for complete survey). Note that the term “physical inactivity” was not included in the survey because there were no suggested changes to the existing SBRN

span.label: a fast-growing field whose central term had a widely-cited definition and a live dispute about its threshold at the same time
span.quote: The definition of sedentary behavior as “any waking behaviour characterized by an energy expenditure ≤1.5 METs while in a sitting or reclining posture,” proposed by SBRN [ 25 ] was widely adopted as evidenced by frequent citations (558 according to SCOPUS, March 20, 2017), though at least one article claimed that there is still not a real consensus on the definition

span.label: **A CONSENSUS DEFINITION AGREED BY 8% OF THE MEMBERSHIP IT WAS SENT TO**: `Our initial invitation ... was sent to ALL 1094 SBRN MEMBERS. Of these, 390 SBRN MEMBERS OPENED THE EMAIL (36%), 134 SBRN MEMBERS (12% of total and 34% of those that opened the email) INDICATED INTEREST, and 87 (8% OF TOTAL and 22% of those that opened the email) COMPLETED THE SURVEY.` The funnel is printed in full, which is the only reason the 8% is visible - and 9 of the 87 were the Steering Committee that drafted the definitions
span.quote: Our initial invitation to participate in the process was sent to all 1094 SBRN members. Of these, 390 SBRN members opened the email (36%), 134 SBRN members (12% of total and 34% of those that opened the email) indicated interest, and 87 (8% of total and 22% of those that opened the email) completed the survey, including Steering Committee members ( n = 9). Respondents were from 20 countries and represented researchers, trainees, graduate students, practitioners and government employees

span.label: AND THE BAR WAS SET BEFORE THE VOTE, WITH ONE TERM EXEMPTED FROM IT: `CONSENSUS WAS DETERMINED A PRIORI to have been achieved IF >=75% OF RESPONDENTS STRONGLY AGREED OR SOMEWHAT AGREED with a particular question ... Note that the term `PHYSICAL INACTIVITY` WAS NOT INCLUDED IN THE SURVEY because there were no suggested changes to the existing SBRN definition.` A fourth consensus threshold in this corpus - after ADQI's two-thirds, CONSORT-AI's 80% and GLIS's >80% - and a term that keeps its definition by not being asked about
span.quote: The survey asked participants to assess the clarity of, and agreement with, the conceptual model and proposed definitions (using a five point scale from strongly agree to strongly disagree), while also providing an opportunity for general comments. Consensus was determined a priori to have been achieved if ≥75% of respondents strongly agreed or somewhat agreed with a particular question (see Additional file 1 : for complete survey). Note that the term “physical inactivity” was not included in the survey because there were no suggested changes to the existing SBRN

span.label: **AND THE DEFINITION HAS TWO COMPONENTS AND NO INSTRUMENT MEASURES BOTH**: `The SBRN definition has DUAL COMPONENTS, including both ENERGY EXPENDITURE and POSTURE. The POSTURAL aspect is easily operationalized ... BUT TENDS TO IGNORE THE ENERGETIC COMPONENT. In contrast, the ENERGETIC aspect, often determined by indirect calorimetry or accelerometry, HAS RECEIVED CRITICISM IN RELATION TO ITS INABILITY TO DISCRIMINATE BETWEEN POSTURES. However, it should be noted that ACCELEROMETERS ASSESS MOVEMENT RATHER THAN ENERGY EXPENDITURE, and therefore AT BEST REPRESENT AN INDIRECT METHOD.` Each instrument sees one half of the definition, and the commonest one sees neither directly
span.quote: The SBRN definition has dual components, including both energy expenditure and posture. The postural aspect is easily operationalized and widely used to identify sedentary behavior using questionnaires, direct observation or inclinometers, but tends to ignore the energetic component. In contrast, the energetic aspect, often determined by indirect calorimetry or accelerometry, has received criticism in relation to its inability to discriminate between postures. However, it should be noted that accelerometers assess movement rather than energy expenditure, and therefore at best represent an indirect method of assessing energy expenditure in any population.

span.label: AND THE CANONICAL INSTANCE FAILS THE CRITERION: `the 1.5 metabolic equivalent (MET) intensity threshold used in the SBRN definition ... was GENERALLY APPROPRIATE for distinguishing between common sitting and standing activities in healthy weight and obese adults; HOWEVER, SOME COMMON SITTING BEHAVIORS (e.g., TYPING) SOMETIMES HAVE A MET LEVEL ABOVE THIS THRESHOLD.` Typing is sitting and typing is not sedentary behaviour, by the definition's own number
span.quote: Mansoubi et al. [ 29 ] concluded that the 1.5 metabolic equivalent (MET) intensity threshold used in the SBRN definition of sedentary behavior was generally appropriate for distinguishing between common sitting and standing activities in healthy weight and obese adults; however, some common sitting behaviors (e.g., typing) sometimes have a MET level above this threshold.

span.label: AND TWO STUDIES REACH OPPOSITE CONCLUSIONS ABOUT THE SAME THRESHOLD FOR THE SAME POPULATION: one reports `that ADULT MET THRESHOLDS MAY NOT BE APPROPRIATE FOR CHILDREN and that the upper limit of the MET threshold for sedentary behavior in children SHOULD BE INCREASED FROM 1.5 TO 2.0 METs`; `IN CONTRAST, using whole-room calorimetry as the criterion measure, Reilly et al. and others concluded that the current MET threshold recommendation of <=1.5 METs SEEMS APPROPRIATE FOR YOUNG CHILDREN`. Same threshold, same population, opposite verdicts, different criterion measures
span.quote: In a recent study that compared MET-defined cut-points used to classify sedentary behaviors in children aged 7–13 years in simulated free-living conditions, it was reported that adult MET thresholds may not be appropriate for children and that the upper limit of the MET threshold for sedentary behavior in children should be increased from 1.5 to 2.0 METs [ 22 ]. These authors suggested that a more precise, age-specific definition of sedentary behavior in children may improve overall physical activity (mis)classification in the population and may be of value in quantifying the health burden of sedentary behaviors in youth. In contrast, using whole-room calorimetry as the criterion measure, Reilly et al. [ 21 ] and others [ 30 ] concluded that the current MET threshold recommendation of ≤1.5 METs seems appropriate for young children (mean age of 5.3 years).

span.label: AND THE ACCELEROMETER CUT-POINT MAY MEAN A DIFFERENT THING IN A DIFFERENT BODY: `While the THRESHOLD OF <=100 cpm is the most commonly used cut-point, Ezeugwu and colleagues suggested that IT MAY ACTUALLY REPRESENT LIGHT INTENSITY ACTIVITY FOR SOME PEOPLE WITH MOBILITY IMPAIRMENT.` The number is the same and the category it names is not - the same shape as this corpus's `the definition names what the assay cannot see`, with the population as the hidden variable
span.quote: There is much debate concerning how to measure sedentary behavior with accelerometers in individuals with different mobility impairments. While the threshold of ≤100 cpm is the most commonly used cut-point [ 35 ], Ezeugwu and colleagues [ 33 ] suggested that it may actually represent light intensity activity for some people with mobility impairment and that there is still a need for further research to determine appropriate accelerometer cut-points among groups with different mobility impairments.

span.label: **AND A CONTROLLED VOCABULARY THAT HAS NOT CAUGHT UP**: `the standardized use of key terms (e.g., sedentary behavior vs physical inactivity) has had VARIABLE UPTAKE ACROSS DISCIPLINES (e.g., behavioral science vs exercise physiology) and MEDICAL SUBJECT HEADINGS (MESH) CONTINUE TO USE PHYSICAL INACTIVITY WHEN SEDENTARY BEHAVIOR WOULD BE MORE APPROPRIATE.` The indexing vocabulary the whole literature is retrieved through is five years behind the distinction the field made
span.quote: There remains, however, a need for further refinement and consensus on a variety of related and emergent terms (e.g., screen time, standing, sitting, reclining), and it has become clear that some commonly used terms are ill-suited for specific populations, such as young children (e.g., before they can sit or stand), those with chronic disease (e.g., hyperthyroidism), or those with mobility impairment (e.g., where postural challenges with standing may represent light or moderate physical activity). Furthermore, the standardized use of key terms (e.g., sedentary behavior vs physical inactivity) has had variable uptake across disciplines (e.g., behavioral science vs exercise physiology) and medical subject headings (MESH) continue to use physical inactivity when sedentary behavior would be more appropriate. Collectively, these issues underscore the need for standardization of terminology, and for definitions that have utility across all ages and physical abilities.

span.label: AND VARYING THE DEFINITION CHANGES WHAT THE VARIABLE PREDICTS: Altenburg and colleagues `examined the occurrence and duration of sedentary bouts, and explored the cross-sectional associations of VARIOUS OPERATIONAL DEFINITIONS of sedentary bouts with health indicators in children. Their study highlighted THE POTENTIAL INFLUENCE OF VARYING DEFINITIONS OF A SEDENTARY BOUT OR SEDENTARY BREAK ON THEIR ASSOCIATION WITH HEALTH INDICATORS, and provided support for the need for a consensus definition of these terms.` The definition is upstream of the finding
span.quote: Altenburg and colleagues [ 18 ] examined the occurrence and duration of sedentary bouts, and explored the cross-sectional associations of various operational definitions of sedentary bouts with health indicators in children. Their study highlighted the potential influence of varying definitions of a sedentary bout or sedentary break on their association with health indicators, and provided support for the need for a consensus definition of these terms.

span.label: AND THE DEFINITION IS BOTH WIDELY ADOPTED AND STILL DISPUTED, IN ONE SENTENCE: `The definition ... proposed by SBRN WAS WIDELY ADOPTED AS EVIDENCED BY FREQUENT CITATIONS (558 ACCORDING TO SCOPUS, March 20, 2017), THOUGH AT LEAST ONE ARTICLE CLAIMED THAT THERE IS STILL NOT A REAL CONSENSUS ON THE DEFINITION.` A citation count offered as evidence of consensus, with the counter-example in the same clause
span.quote: The definition of sedentary behavior as “any waking behaviour characterized by an energy expenditure ≤1.5 METs while in a sitting or reclining posture,” proposed by SBRN [ 25 ] was widely adopted as evidenced by frequent citations (558 according to SCOPUS, March 20, 2017), though at least one article claimed that there is still not a real consensus on the definition

span.label: AND THE PREVIOUS DEFINITION TRAVELLED BY TRANSLATION: `In 2012, the Sedentary Behaviour Research Network published a letter proposing definitions AIMED AT CLARIFYING DIFFERENCES BETWEEN `SEDENTARY BEHAVIOUR` AND `PHYSICAL INACTIVITY`. This clarification, AUTHORED BY 52 SBRN MEMBERS, achieved wide acceptance and was published in English and WAS SUBSEQUENTLY TRANSLATED AND PUBLISHED IN FRENCH`, Portuguese and Spanish. A definition propagated by translation, with the author count as its warrant
span.quote: In 2012, the Sedentary Behaviour Research Network (SBRN; a network connecting sedentary behavior researchers and health professionals from around the world interested in sedentary behavior research [ 24 ]) published a letter proposing definitions aimed at clarifying differences between “sedentary behaviour” and “physical inactivity” [ 25 ]. This clarification, authored by 52 SBRN members, achieved wide acceptance and was published in English [ 25 , 26 ] and was subsequently translated and published in French

span.label: THE FIELD HAS SEVERAL SIMULTANEOUS STANDARDISATION PROJECTS AND NO AGREED DEFINITIONS: `Several other large-scale projects are currently underway to produce A COMMON TAXONOMY, HARMONIZED MEASUREMENT PROTOCOLS, CONSISTENT DATA REDUCTION AND ANALYTIC PROCEDURES, and a framework for establishing research priorities. However, A COLLABORATIVE GLOBAL INITIATIVE TO ARRIVE AT CONSENSUS DEFINITIONS ON KEY TERMS HAS REMAINED ELUSIVE.` Five named initiatives - AlPHABET, ISMPB, ISPAH, the Sensor Methods Collaboratory, SIT, SOS - and the definitions were still open
span.quote: Several other large-scale projects are currently underway to produce a common taxonomy, harmonized measurement protocols, consistent data reduction and analytic procedures, and a framework for establishing research priorities (Table 2 ). However, a collaborative global initiative to arrive at consensus definitions on key terms has remained elusive.

span.label: AND THE TERMS ARE ILL-SUITED TO SOME OF THE PEOPLE THEY DESCRIBE: `it has become clear that SOME COMMONLY USED TERMS ARE ILL-SUITED FOR SPECIFIC POPULATIONS, such as YOUNG CHILDREN (e.g., BEFORE THEY CAN SIT OR STAND), those with chronic disease (e.g., hyperthyroidism), or those with MOBILITY IMPAIRMENT (e.g., WHERE POSTURAL CHALLENGES WITH STANDING MAY REPRESENT LIGHT OR MODERATE PHYSICAL ACTIVITY).` A definition built on posture excludes, by construction, everyone whose posture does not mean what it assumes
span.quote: There remains, however, a need for further refinement and consensus on a variety of related and emergent terms (e.g., screen time, standing, sitting, reclining), and it has become clear that some commonly used terms are ill-suited for specific populations, such as young children (e.g., before they can sit or stand), those with chronic disease (e.g., hyperthyroidism), or those with mobility impairment (e.g., where postural challenges with standing may represent light or moderate physical activity). Furthermore, the standardized use of key terms (e.g., sedentary behavior vs physical inactivity) has had variable uptake across disciplines (e.g., behavioral science vs exercise physiology) and medical subject headings (MESH) continue to use physical inactivity when sedentary behavior would be more appropriate. Collectively, these issues underscore the need for standardization of terminology, and for definitions that have utility across all ages and physical abilities.

span.label: and the evidence base narrowed sharply: `The literature search identified 997 ARTICLES, and after screening for inclusion criteria, 14 WERE USED for the identification and definition of key terms.` Fourteen papers behind a terminology for a field publishing at the rate this one does
span.quote: The literature search identified 997 articles, and after screening for inclusion criteria, 14 were used for the identification and definition of key terms in sedentary behavior research.

This clarification, authored by 52 SBRN members, achieved wide acceptance and was published in English [ 25 , 26 ] and was subsequently translated and published in French

span.label: postural aspect
span.quote: The SBRN definition has dual components, including both energy expenditure and posture. The postural aspect is easily operationalized and widely used to identify sedentary behavior using questionnaires, direct observation or inclinometers, but tends to ignore the energetic component. In contrast, the energetic aspect, often determined by indirect calorimetry or accelerometry, has received criticism in relation to its inability to discriminate between postures. However, it should be noted that accelerometers assess movement rather than energy expenditure, and therefore at best represent an indirect method of assessing energy expenditure in any population.

span.quote: The SBRN definition has dual components, including both energy expenditure and posture. The postural aspect is easily operationalized and widely used to identify sedentary behavior using questionnaires, direct observation or inclinometers, but tends to ignore the energetic component. In contrast, the energetic aspect, often determined by indirect calorimetry or accelerometry, has received criticism in relation to its inability to discriminate between postures. However, it should be noted that accelerometers assess movement rather than energy expenditure, and therefore at best represent an indirect method of assessing energy expenditure in any population.

span.term: AND TWO STUDIES REACH OPPOSITE CONCLUSIONS ON THE SAME THRESHOLD FOR CHILDREN: `the upper limit ... SHOULD BE INCREASED FROM 1.5 TO 2.0 METs` against `the current MET threshold recommendation of <=1.5 METs SEEMS APPROPRIATE FOR YOUNG CHILDREN`
span.quote: In a recent study that compared MET-defined cut-points used to classify sedentary behaviors in children aged 7–13 years in simulated free-living conditions, it was reported that adult MET thresholds may not be appropriate for children and that the upper limit of the MET threshold for sedentary behavior in children should be increased from 1.5 to 2.0 METs [ 22 ]. These authors suggested that a more precise, age-specific definition of sedentary behavior in children may improve overall physical activity (mis)classification in the population and may be of value in quantifying the health burden of sedentary behaviors in youth. In contrast, using whole-room calorimetry as the criterion measure, Reilly et al. [ 21 ] and others [ 30 ] concluded that the current MET threshold recommendation of ≤1.5 METs seems appropriate for young children (mean age of 5.3 years).

span.label: **AND A CONTROLLED VOCABULARY THAT HAS NOT CAUGHT UP**: `MEDICAL SUBJECT HEADINGS (MESH) CONTINUE TO USE PHYSICAL INACTIVITY WHEN SEDENTARY BEHAVIOR WOULD BE MORE APPROPRIATE`
span.term: **AND A CONTROLLED VOCABULARY THAT HAS NOT CAUGHT UP**: `MEDICAL SUBJECT HEADINGS (MESH) CONTINUE TO USE PHYSICAL INACTIVITY WHEN SEDENTARY BEHAVIOR WOULD BE MORE APPROPRIATE`
span.quote: There remains, however, a need for further refinement and consensus on a variety of related and emergent terms (e.g., screen time, standing, sitting, reclining), and it has become clear that some commonly used terms are ill-suited for specific populations, such as young children (e.g., before they can sit or stand), those with chronic disease (e.g., hyperthyroidism), or those with mobility impairment (e.g., where postural challenges with standing may represent light or moderate physical activity). Furthermore, the standardized use of key terms (e.g., sedentary behavior vs physical inactivity) has had variable uptake across disciplines (e.g., behavioral science vs exercise physiology) and medical subject headings (MESH) continue to use physical inactivity when sedentary behavior would be more appropriate. Collectively, these issues underscore the need for standardization of terminology, and for definitions that have utility across all ages and physical abilities.

Their study highlighted the potential influence of varying definitions of a sedentary bout or sedentary break on their association with health indicators, and provided support for the need for a consensus definition of these terms.

span.term: MET ceiling for sedentary behaviour, across the literature
span.quote: As this field of research has grown, so too has confusion over the definition of sedentary behavior (see Table 1 for a sample of definitions) and other related terms (e.g., screen time, sedentary behavior patterns, bouts, breaks) [ 4 , 7 , 17 – 22 ]. For example, Altenburg and Chinapaw [ 17 ] recently recommended that to advance the field of sedentary behavior epidemiology, standardized procedures for accelerometer data collection and data reduction should be defined; standardized operational definitions of sedentary bouts and breaks are needed; sedentary bouts should be operationally defined as a minimum period of uninterrupted sedentary time; total time accumulated in sedentary bouts per day (or per week) should be calculated rather than using average bout duration; and the best mathematical adjustment that converts accelerometer data into sedentary patterns should be further explored.
